## Scan execution checklist

| Recipe | Hits (relevant) |
|---|---|
| `.ToLower()` / `.ToUpper()` | 3 (L79 ×2, L121) |
| `.Substring(` | 2 (L79) |
| Chained `.Replace(` | Underscore L117-121, Titleize L58-60 |
| `RegexOptions.Compiled` | 5 fields (L26-28, 36-38) + InflectionRule L215 |
| `new Regex(` | 4 (L26-28, L215) |
| `GeneratedRegex` | 3 ✅ (L13,16,19) |
| Regex replace with closure (per-match alloc) | 1 (Pascalize L78-79) |
| `public/internal class` unsealed | 1 (`InflectionRule` L200) |

## Findings

#### 1. `Underscore` — triple compiled-regex chain + culture `.ToLower()` (🔴 Critical on hot path)
**Impact:** 4 string allocations per call (3 regex intermediates + `ToLower`) plus 3 sequential regex passes. At millions of calls this dominates the pipeline. `.ToLower()` is also culture-sensitive → correctness bug (Turkish-I).
**Files:** `CaseTransformExtensions.cs:L115-121`, regex fields `L36-38`
**Fix:** Replace the whole thing with a single-pass manual `char` scan over a `Span<char>`/`stackalloc` buffer, appending `_` on case boundaries and lowering via `char.ToLowerInvariant`. Eliminates all 3 regexes and all 4 allocations (1 final string alloc only). At minimum, change `.ToLower()` → `.ToLowerInvariant()`.

Example single-pass replacement:
```csharp
public static string Underscore(this string input)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(input)) return input;
    var sb = new StringBuilder(input.Length + 8);
    for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
    {
        char c = input[i];
        if (c is '-' or ' ') { sb.Append('_'); continue; }
        if (char.IsUpper(c) && i > 0)
        {
            char prev = input[i - 1];
            bool nextLower = i + 1 < input.Length && char.IsLower(input[i + 1]);
            if (char.IsLower(prev) || char.IsDigit(prev) || (char.IsUpper(prev) && nextLower))
                sb.Append('_');
        }
        sb.Append(char.ToLowerInvariant(c));
    }
    return sb.ToString();
}
```
**Caveat:** Verify against your test cases (`HTMLParser` → `html_parser`, digit boundaries); the manual boundary logic must reproduce both `UnderscoreRegex1`/`2` semantics.

#### 2. `Pascalize` — closure allocates a string per regex match (🔴 Critical on hot path)
**Impact:** `MatchEvaluator` delegate runs per match; each match does `Substring(0,1)` + `ToUpper()` + `Substring(1)` + `+` = **4 allocations per word**, times N words, times millions of calls. `.ToUpper()` is culture-sensitive.
**Files:** `CaseTransformExtensions.cs:L78-79`
**Fix:** Enumerate `WordPartsRegex().EnumerateMatches(input)` (or `Match`/`NextMatch`) into a pooled/`StringBuilder` buffer, writing `char.ToUpperInvariant(span[0])` then the remaining span directly — zero per-match substrings. Also fixes the culture bug via `ToUpperInvariant`.

#### 3. `Camelize` — extra full Pascalize allocation + `[1..]` slice (🟡 Moderate, escalated on hot path)
**Impact:** Allocates the full Pascalized string, then `pascalized[1..]` allocates a second string just to change one char.
**Files:** `CaseTransformExtensions.cs:L93-101`
**Fix:** After building the Pascalized buffer (finding #2), lower only index 0 in the buffer before materializing — avoids the second allocation entirely. If keeping current structure, this is unavoidable; fold Camelize into the shared buffer builder.

#### 4. `Kebaberize` — inherits Underscore cost + extra `Replace` (🟡 Moderate)
**Impact:** Full `Underscore` cost (finding #1) plus a `Dasherize` `.Replace('_','-')` allocation. Fixing #1 mostly resolves this; ideally emit `-` directly instead of `_`-then-replace.
**Files:** `CaseTransformExtensions.cs:L147-149`, `L133-134`

#### 5. `InflectionRule` — 40-60 `RegexOptions.Compiled` at startup, unsealed (ℹ️ Info / startup)
**Impact:** Comment notes 40-60 compiled regexes → 100-500ms JIT/startup cost for matching short strings; `Compiled` rarely pays off for short inputs. Class is also unsealed.
**Files:** `CaseTransformExtensions.cs:L215`, class decl `L200`
**Fix:** Drop `RegexOptions.Compiled` (keep `IgnoreCase`), or use `GeneratedRegex` where patterns are literals. Mark `sealed class InflectionRule`.

## Positive findings
- ✅ `GeneratedRegex` used for the 3 core regexes (`L13,16,19`) — correct source-gen approach.
- ✅ `Slugify` uses `ToLowerInvariant` (`L189`) — culture-correct.
- ✅ `IsAllUpperCase`/`WordCount`/`IsAsciiAlphanumeric` use `foreach` char scans, no LINQ (`L159,252,277`).

| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | 2 | `Underscore` triple-regex+ToLower chain (4 allocs/call) |
| 🟡 Moderate | 2 | `Camelize` double allocation; `Kebaberize` extra Replace |
| ℹ️ Info | 1 | `InflectionRule` compiled-regex startup budget |

The two 🔴 items (`Underscore`, `Pascalize`) are where your millions-of-calls pipeline will see the biggest win — both eliminate per-call/per-match allocations and also fix latent culture-sensitivity bugs.

> ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** These results are generated by an AI assistant and are non-deterministic. Findings may include false positives or miss real issues. Verify with benchmarks (BenchmarkDotNet) and human review before applying to production.

# .NET Performance Patterns

Scan C#/.NET code for performance anti-patterns and produce prioritized findings with concrete fixes. Patterns sourced from the official .NET performance blog series, distilled to customer-actionable guidance.

## When to Use

- Reviewing C#/.NET code for performance optimization opportunities
- Auditing hot paths for allocation-heavy or inefficient patterns
- Systematic scan of a codebase for known anti-patterns before release
- Second-opinion analysis after manual performance review

## When Not to Use

- **Algorithmic complexity analysis** — this skill targets API usage patterns, not algorithm design
- **Code not on a hot path** with no performance requirements — avoid premature optimization

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Source code | Yes | C# files, code blocks, or repository paths to scan |
| Hot-path context | Recommended | Which code paths are performance-critical |
| Target framework | Recommended | .NET version (some patterns require .NET 8+) |
| Scan depth | Optional | `critical-only`, `standard` (default), or `comprehensive` |

## Workflow

### Step 1: Load Reference Files (if available)

Try to load `references/critical-patterns.md` and the topic-specific reference files listed below. These contain detailed detection recipes and grep commands.

**If reference files are not found** (e.g., in a sandboxed environment or when the skill is embedded as instructions only), **skip file loading and proceed directly to Step 3** using the scan recipes listed inline below. Do not spend time searching the filesystem for reference files — if they aren't at the expected relative path, they aren't available.

### Step 2: Detect Code Signals and Select Topic Recipes

Scan the code for signals that indicate which pattern categories to check. If reference files were loaded, use their `## Detection` sections. Otherwise, use the inline recipes in Step 3.

| Signal in Code | Topic |
|----------------|-------|
| `async`, `await`, `Task`, `ValueTask` | Async patterns |
| `Span<`, `Memory<`, `stackalloc`, `ArrayPool`, `string.Substring`, `.Replace(`, `.ToLower()`, `+=` in loops, `params` | Memory & strings |
| `Regex`, `[GeneratedRegex]`, `Regex.Match`, `RegexOptions.Compiled` | Regex patterns |
| `Dictionary<`, `List<`, `.ToList()`, `.Where(`, `.Select(`, LINQ methods, `static readonly Dictionary<` | Collections & LINQ |
| `JsonSerializer`, `HttpClient`, `Stream`, `FileStream` | I/O & serialization |

Always check structural patterns (unsealed classes) regardless of signals.

**Scan depth controls scope:**
- `critical-only`: Only critical patterns (deadlocks, >10x regressions)
- `standard` (default): Critical + detected topic patterns
- `comprehensive`: All pattern categories

### Step 3: Scan and Report

**For files under 500 lines, read the entire file first** — you'll spot most patterns faster than running individual grep recipes. Use grep to confirm counts and catch patterns you might miss visually.

For each relevant pattern category, run the detection recipes below. Report exact counts, not estimates.

**Core scan recipes** (run these when reference files aren't available):
```
# Strings & memory
grep -n '\.IndexOf(\"' FILE                    # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.Substring(' FILE                    # Substring allocations
grep -En '\.(StartsWith|EndsWith|Contains)\s*\(' FILE  # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.ToLower()\|\.ToUpper()' FILE        # Culture-sensitive + allocation
grep -n '\.Replace(' FILE                      # Chained Replace allocations
grep -n 'params ' FILE                         # params array allocation

# Collections & LINQ
grep -n '\.Select\|\.Where\|\.OrderBy\|\.GroupBy' FILE  # LINQ on hot path
grep -n '\.All\|\.Any' FILE                    # LINQ on string/char
grep -n 'new Dictionary<\|new List<' FILE      # Per-call allocation
grep -n 'static readonly Dictionary<' FILE     # FrozenDictionary candidate

# Regex
grep -n 'RegexOptions.Compiled' FILE           # Compiled regex budget
grep -n 'new Regex(' FILE                      # Per-call regex
grep -n 'GeneratedRegex' FILE                  # Positive: source-gen regex

# Structural
grep -n 'public class \|internal class ' FILE  # Unsealed classes
grep -n 'sealed class' FILE                    # Already sealed
grep -n ': IEquatable' FILE                    # Positive: struct equality
```

**Rules:**
- Run every relevant recipe for the detected pattern categories
- **Emit a scan execution checklist** before classifying findings — list each recipe and the hit count
- A result of **0 hits** is valid and valuable (confirms good practice)
- If reference files were loaded, also run their `## Detection` recipes

**Verify-the-Inverse Rule:** For absence patterns, always count both sides and report the ratio (e.g., "N of M classes are sealed"). The ratio determines severity — 0/185 is systematic, 12/15 is a consistency fix.

### Step 3b: Cross-File Consistency Check

If an optimized pattern is found in one file, check whether sibling files (same directory, same interface, same base class) use the un-optimized equivalent. Flag as 🟡 Moderate with the optimized file as evidence.

### Step 3c: Compound Allocation Check

After running scan recipes, look for these multi-allocation patterns that single-line recipes miss:

1. **Branched `.Replace()` chains:** Methods that call `.Replace()` across multiple `if/else` branches — report total allocation count across all branches, not just per-line.
2. **Cross-method chaining:** When a public method delegates to another method that itself allocates intermediates (e.g., A calls B which does 3 regex replaces, then A calls C), report the total chain cost as one finding.
3. **Compound `+=` with embedded allocating calls:** Lines like `result += $"...{Foo().ToLower()}"` are 2+ allocations (interpolation + ToLower + concatenation) — flag the compound cost, not just the `.ToLower()`.
4. **`string.Format` specificity:** Distinguish resource-loaded format strings (not fixable) from compile-time literal format strings (fixable with interpolation). Enumerate the actionable sites.

### Step 4: Classify and Prioritize Findings

Assign each finding a severity:

| Severity | Criteria | Action |
|----------|----------|--------|
| 🔴 **Critical** | Deadlocks, crashes, security vulnerabilities, >10x regression | Must fix |
| 🟡 **Moderate** | 2-10x improvement opportunity, best practice for hot paths | Should fix on hot paths |
| ℹ️ **Info** | Pattern applies but code may not be on a hot path | Consider if profiling shows impact |

**Prioritization rules:**
1. If the user identified hot-path code, elevate all findings in that code to their maximum severity
2. If hot-path context is unknown, report 🔴 Critical findings unconditionally; report 🟡 Moderate findings with a note: _"Impactful if this code is on a hot path"_
3. Never suggest micro-optimizations on code that is clearly not performance-sensitive

**Scale-based severity escalation:**
When the same pattern appears across many instances, escalate severity:
- 1-10 instances of the same anti-pattern → report at the pattern's base severity
- 11-50 instances → escalate ℹ️ Info patterns to 🟡 Moderate
- 50+ instances → escalate to 🟡 Moderate with elevated priority; flag as a codebase-wide systematic issue

Always report exact counts (from scan recipes), not estimates or agent summaries.

### Step 5: Generate Findings

**Keep findings compact.** Each finding is one short block — not an essay. Group by severity (🔴 → 🟡 → ℹ️), not by file.

Format per finding:

```
#### ID. Title (N instances)
**Impact:** one-line impact statement
**Files:** file1.cs:L1, file2.cs:L2, ... (list locations, don't build tables)
**Fix:** one-line description of the change (e.g., "Add `StringComparison.Ordinal` parameter")
**Caveat:** only if non-obvious (version requirement, correctness risk)
```

**Rules for compact output:**
- **No ❌/✅ code blocks** for trivial fixes (adding a keyword, parameter, or type change). A one-line fix description suffices.
- **Only include code blocks** for non-obvious transformations (e.g., replacing a LINQ chain with a foreach loop, or hoisting a closure).
- **File locations as inline comma-separated list**, not a table. Use `File.cs:L42` format.
- **No explanatory prose** beyond the Impact line — the severity icon already conveys urgency.
- **Merge related findings** that share the same fix (e.g., all `.ToLower()` calls go in one finding, not split by file).
- **Positive findings** in a bullet list, not a table. One line per pattern: `✅ Pattern — evidence`.

End with a summary table and disclaimer:

```markdown
| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | N | ... |
| 🟡 Moderate | N | ... |
| ℹ️ Info | N | ... |

> ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** These results are generated by an AI assistant and are non-deterministic. Findings may include false positives, miss real issues, or suggest changes that are incorrect for your specific context. Always verify recommendations with benchmarks and human review before applying changes to production code.
```

## Validation

Before delivering results, verify:

- [ ] All critical patterns were checked (from reference files or inline recipes)
- [ ] Topic-specific recipes run only when matching signals detected
- [ ] Each finding includes a concrete code fix
- [ ] Scan execution checklist is complete (all recipes run)
- [ ] Summary table included at end

## Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Correct Approach |
|---------|-----------------|
| Flagging every `Dictionary` as needing `FrozenDictionary` | Only flag if the dictionary is never mutated after construction |
| Suggesting `Span<T>` in async methods | Use `Memory<T>` in async code; `Span<T>` only in sync hot paths |
| Reporting LINQ outside hot paths | Only flag LINQ in identified hot paths or tight loops; LINQ is acceptable in code that runs infrequently. Since .NET 7, LINQ Min/Max/Sum/Average are vectorized — blanket bans on LINQ are misguided |
| Suggesting `ConfigureAwait(false)` in app code | Only applicable in library code; not primarily a performance concern |
| Recommending `ValueTask` everywhere | Only for hot paths with frequent synchronous completion |
| Flagging `new HttpClient()` in DI services | Check if `IHttpClientFactory` is already in use |
| Suggesting `[GeneratedRegex]` for dynamic patterns | Only flag when the pattern string is a compile-time literal |
| Suggesting `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan` broadly | Only for ultra-hot paths with benchmarked evidence; adds complexity and fragility |
| Suggesting `unsafe` code for micro-optimizations | Avoid `unsafe` except where absolutely necessary — do not recommend it for micro-optimizations that don't matter. Safe alternatives like `Span<T>`, `stackalloc` in safe context, and `ArrayPool` cover the vast majority of performance needs |

</skill-context>

### 🔴 Critical

#### 1. Double regex evaluation on every rule, every request (1 site, amplified ×46 rules)
**Impact:** `Apply` runs the regex **twice** per rule — `IsMatch` then `Replace`. `Pluralize`/`Singularize` scans up to 46 rules until one matches, so a single request can trigger dozens of redundant regex executions. This is the dominant per-request cost.
**Files:** `WordVocabulary.cs:182-187`
**Fix:** Match once and reuse the result:
```csharp
public string? Apply(string word)
{
    var match = _regex.Match(word);
    return match.Success ? _regex.Replace(word, _replacement) : null;
}
```
Better still, eliminate the second pass entirely with `match.Result(_replacement)` when patterns are single-match (all here are `$`-anchored):
```csharp
var match = _regex.Match(word);
if (!match.Success) return null;
return string.Concat(word.AsSpan(0, match.Index), match.Result(_replacement), word.AsSpan(match.Index + match.Length));
```

---

### 🟡 Moderate

#### 2. `CurrentCultureIgnoreCase` on hot-path HashSet lookups (1 site)
**Impact:** Every `Pluralize`/`Singularize`/`IsUncountable` call does `_uncountables.Contains(...)`; culture-sensitive comparison is ~3–4× slower than ordinal and allocates culture data. Your own comment already flags this, and the irregulars maps correctly use `OrdinalIgnoreCase`.
**Files:** `WordVocabulary.cs:17`
**Fix:** Change to `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` (matches the two irregular dictionaries).

#### 3. `RegexOptions.Compiled` × 46 dynamic regexes — startup cost (1 site)
**Impact:** `Compiled` JITs each pattern at construction (~100–500ms across 46 rules, per the code comment) and increases memory. Since patterns in `DefaultInflections` are **compile-time literals**, they're candidates for source-generated regex (zero startup JIT, best steady-state throughput).
**Files:** `WordVocabulary.cs:176`, patterns at `WordVocabulary.cs:208-252`
**Fix:** If startup latency matters, prefer `[GeneratedRegex]` for the default set (requires restructuring away from the `string`→`Regex` factory). If per-request latency dominates and startup is acceptable, keep `Compiled`. Do **not** keep `Compiled` for regexes built from arbitrary runtime input.
**Caveat:** `[GeneratedRegex]` needs .NET 7+ and literal patterns; it can't be applied to the current string-based `AddPlural` path without refactoring.

#### 4. Unsealed classes (2 of 2 unsealed)
**Impact:** `WordVocabulary` and the internal `InflectionEntry` are unsealed. Sealing `InflectionEntry` lets the JIT devirtualize/inline `Apply`, which is invoked in the hot loop.

# .NET Performance Patterns

Scan C#/.NET code for performance anti-patterns and produce prioritized findings with concrete fixes. Patterns sourced from the official .NET performance blog series, distilled to customer-actionable guidance.

## When to Use

- Reviewing C#/.NET code for performance optimization opportunities
- Auditing hot paths for allocation-heavy or inefficient patterns
- Systematic scan of a codebase for known anti-patterns before release
- Second-opinion analysis after manual performance review

## When Not to Use

- **Algorithmic complexity analysis** — this skill targets API usage patterns, not algorithm design
- **Code not on a hot path** with no performance requirements — avoid premature optimization

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Source code | Yes | C# files, code blocks, or repository paths to scan |
| Hot-path context | Recommended | Which code paths are performance-critical |
| Target framework | Recommended | .NET version (some patterns require .NET 8+) |
| Scan depth | Optional | `critical-only`, `standard` (default), or `comprehensive` |

## Workflow

### Step 1: Load Reference Files (if available)

Try to load `references/critical-patterns.md` and the topic-specific reference files listed below. These contain detailed detection recipes and grep commands.

**If reference files are not found** (e.g., in a sandboxed environment or when the skill is embedded as instructions only), **skip file loading and proceed directly to Step 3** using the scan recipes listed inline below. Do not spend time searching the filesystem for reference files — if they aren't at the expected relative path, they aren't available.

### Step 2: Detect Code Signals and Select Topic Recipes

Scan the code for signals that indicate which pattern categories to check. If reference files were loaded, use their `## Detection` sections. Otherwise, use the inline recipes in Step 3.

| Signal in Code | Topic |
|----------------|-------|
| `async`, `await`, `Task`, `ValueTask` | Async patterns |
| `Span<`, `Memory<`, `stackalloc`, `ArrayPool`, `string.Substring`, `.Replace(`, `.ToLower()`, `+=` in loops, `params` | Memory & strings |
| `Regex`, `[GeneratedRegex]`, `Regex.Match`, `RegexOptions.Compiled` | Regex patterns |
| `Dictionary<`, `List<`, `.ToList()`, `.Where(`, `.Select(`, LINQ methods, `static readonly Dictionary<` | Collections & LINQ |
| `JsonSerializer`, `HttpClient`, `Stream`, `FileStream` | I/O & serialization |

Always check structural patterns (unsealed classes) regardless of signals.

**Scan depth controls scope:**
- `critical-only`: Only critical patterns (deadlocks, >10x regressions)
- `standard` (default): Critical + detected topic patterns
- `comprehensive`: All pattern categories

### Step 3: Scan and Report

**For files under 500 lines, read the entire file first** — you'll spot most patterns faster than running individual grep recipes. Use grep to confirm counts and catch patterns you might miss visually.

For each relevant pattern category, run the detection recipes below. Report exact counts, not estimates.

**Core scan recipes** (run these when reference files aren't available):

grep -En '\.(StartsWith|EndsWith|Contains)\s*\(' FILE  # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.ToLower()\|\.ToUpper()' FILE        # Culture-sensitive + allocation
grep -n '\.Replace(' FILE                      # Chained Replace allocations
grep -n 'params ' FILE                         # params array allocation

grep -n '\.All\|\.Any' FILE                    # LINQ on string/char
grep -n 'new Dictionary<\|new List<' FILE      # Per-call allocation
grep -n 'static readonly Dictionary<' FILE     # FrozenDictionary candidate

# Regex

grep -n 'new Regex(' FILE                      # Per-call regex
grep -n 'GeneratedRegex' FILE                  # Positive: source-gen regex

**Files:** `WordVocabulary.cs:182-187`
**Fix:** Match once and reuse the result:
```csharp
public string? Apply(string word)
{
    var match = _regex.Match(word);
    return match.Success ? _regex.Replace(word, _replacement) : null;
}
```
Better still, eliminate the second pass entirely with `match.Result(_replacement)` when patterns are single-match (all here are `$`-anchored):
```csharp
var match = _regex.Match(word);
if (!match.Success) return null;
return string.Concat(word.AsSpan(0, match.Index), match.Result(_replacement), word.AsSpan(match.Index + match.Length));
```

#### 2. `CurrentCultureIgnoreCase` on hot-path HashSet lookups (1 site)

**Files:** `WordVocabulary.cs:17`
**Fix:** Change to `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` (matches the two irregular dictionaries).

#### 3. `RegexOptions.Compiled` × 46 dynamic regexes — startup cost (1 site)
**Impact:** `Compiled` JITs each pattern at construction (~100–500ms across 46 rules, per the code comment) and increases memory. Since patterns in `DefaultInflections` are **compile-time literals**, they're candidates for source-generated regex (zero startup JIT, best steady-state throughput).

# .NET Performance Patterns

Scan C#/.NET code for performance anti-patterns and produce prioritized findings with concrete fixes. Patterns sourced from the official .NET performance blog series, distilled to customer-actionable guidance.

## When to Use

- Reviewing C#/.NET code for performance optimization opportunities
- Auditing hot paths for allocation-heavy or inefficient patterns
- Systematic scan of a codebase for known anti-patterns before release
- Second-opinion analysis after manual performance review

## When Not to Use

- **Algorithmic complexity analysis** — this skill targets API usage patterns, not algorithm design
- **Code not on a hot path** with no performance requirements — avoid premature optimization

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Source code | Yes | C# files, code blocks, or repository paths to scan |
| Hot-path context | Recommended | Which code paths are performance-critical |
| Target framework | Recommended | .NET version (some patterns require .NET 8+) |
| Scan depth | Optional | `critical-only`, `standard` (default), or `comprehensive` |

## Workflow

### Step 1: Load Reference Files (if available)

Try to load `references/critical-patterns.md` and the topic-specific reference files listed below. These contain detailed detection recipes and grep commands.

**If reference files are not found** (e.g., in a sandboxed environment or when the skill is embedded as instructions only), **skip file loading and proceed directly to Step 3** using the scan recipes listed inline below. Do not spend time searching the filesystem for reference files — if they aren't at the expected relative path, they aren't available.

### Step 2: Detect Code Signals and Select Topic Recipes

Scan the code for signals that indicate which pattern categories to check. If reference files were loaded, use their `## Detection` sections. Otherwise, use the inline recipes in Step 3.

| Signal in Code | Topic |
|----------------|-------|
| `async`, `await`, `Task`, `ValueTask` | Async patterns |
| `Span<`, `Memory<`, `stackalloc`, `ArrayPool`, `string.Substring`, `.Replace(`, `.ToLower()`, `+=` in loops, `params` | Memory & strings |
| `Regex`, `[GeneratedRegex]`, `Regex.Match`, `RegexOptions.Compiled` | Regex patterns |
| `Dictionary<`, `List<`, `.ToList()`, `.Where(`, `.Select(`, LINQ methods, `static readonly Dictionary<` | Collections & LINQ |
| `JsonSerializer`, `HttpClient`, `Stream`, `FileStream` | I/O & serialization |

Always check structural patterns (unsealed classes) regardless of signals.

**Scan depth controls scope:**
- `critical-only`: Only critical patterns (deadlocks, >10x regressions)
- `standard` (default): Critical + detected topic patterns
- `comprehensive`: All pattern categories

### Step 3: Scan and Report

**For files under 500 lines, read the entire file first** — you'll spot most patterns faster than running individual grep recipes. Use grep to confirm counts and catch patterns you might miss visually.

For each relevant pattern category, run the detection recipes below. Report exact counts, not estimates.

**Core scan recipes** (run these when reference files aren't available):
```
# Strings & memory
grep -n '\.IndexOf(\"' FILE                    # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.Substring(' FILE                    # Substring allocations
grep -En '\.(StartsWith|EndsWith|Contains)\s*\(' FILE  # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.ToLower()\|\.ToUpper()' FILE        # Culture-sensitive + allocation
grep -n '\.Replace(' FILE                      # Chained Replace allocations
grep -n 'params ' FILE                         # params array allocation

# Collections & LINQ
grep -n '\.Select\|\.Where\|\.OrderBy\|\.GroupBy' FILE  # LINQ on hot path
grep -n '\.All\|\.Any' FILE                    # LINQ on string/char
grep -n 'new Dictionary<\|new List<' FILE      # Per-call allocation
grep -n 'static readonly Dictionary<' FILE     # FrozenDictionary candidate

# Regex
grep -n 'RegexOptions.Compiled' FILE           # Compiled regex budget
grep -n 'new Regex(' FILE                      # Per-call regex
grep -n 'GeneratedRegex' FILE                  # Positive: source-gen regex

# Structural
grep -n 'public class \|internal class ' FILE  # Unsealed classes
grep -n 'sealed class' FILE                    # Already sealed
grep -n ': IEquatable' FILE                    # Positive: struct equality
```

**Rules:**
- Run every relevant recipe for the detected pattern categories
- **Emit a scan execution checklist** before classifying findings — list each recipe and the hit count
- A result of **0 hits** is valid and valuable (confirms good practice)
- If reference files were loaded, also run their `## Detection` recipes

**Verify-the-Inverse Rule:** For absence patterns, always count both sides and report the ratio (e.g., "N of M classes are sealed"). The ratio determines severity — 0/185 is systematic, 12/15 is a consistency fix.

### Step 3b: Cross-File Consistency Check

If an optimized pattern is found in one file, check whether sibling files (same directory, same interface, same base class) use the un-optimized equivalent. Flag as 🟡 Moderate with the optimized file as evidence.

### Step 3c: Compound Allocation Check

After running scan recipes, look for these multi-allocation patterns that single-line recipes miss:

1. **Branched `.Replace()` chains:** Methods that call `.Replace()` across multiple `if/else` branches — report total allocation count across all branches, not just per-line.
2. **Cross-method chaining:** When a public method delegates to another method that itself allocates intermediates (e.g., A calls B which does 3 regex replaces, then A calls C), report the total chain cost as one finding.
3. **Compound `+=` with embedded allocating calls:** Lines like `result += $"...{Foo().ToLower()}"` are 2+ allocations (interpolation + ToLower + concatenation) — flag the compound cost, not just the `.ToLower()`.
4. **`string.Format` specificity:** Distinguish resource-loaded format strings (not fixable) from compile-time literal format strings (fixable with interpolation). Enumerate the actionable sites.

### Step 4: Classify and Prioritize Findings

Assign each finding a severity:

| Severity | Criteria | Action |
|----------|----------|--------|
| 🔴 **Critical** | Deadlocks, crashes, security vulnerabilities, >10x regression | Must fix |
| 🟡 **Moderate** | 2-10x improvement opportunity, best practice for hot paths | Should fix on hot paths |
| ℹ️ **Info** | Pattern applies but code may not be on a hot path | Consider if profiling shows impact |

**Prioritization rules:**
1. If the user identified hot-path code, elevate all findings in that code to their maximum severity
2. If hot-path context is unknown, report 🔴 Critical findings unconditionally; report 🟡 Moderate findings with a note: _"Impactful if this code is on a hot path"_
3. Never suggest micro-optimizations on code that is clearly not performance-sensitive

**Scale-based severity escalation:**
When the same pattern appears across many instances, escalate severity:
- 1-10 instances of the same anti-pattern → report at the pattern's base severity
- 11-50 instances → escalate ℹ️ Info patterns to 🟡 Moderate
- 50+ instances → escalate to 🟡 Moderate with elevated priority; flag as a codebase-wide systematic issue

Always report exact counts (from scan recipes), not estimates or agent summaries.

### Step 5: Generate Findings

**Keep findings compact.** Each finding is one short block — not an essay. Group by severity (🔴 → 🟡 → ℹ️), not by file.

Format per finding:

```
#### ID. Title (N instances)
**Impact:** one-line impact statement
**Files:** file1.cs:L1, file2.cs:L2, ... (list locations, don't build tables)
**Fix:** one-line description of the change (e.g., "Add `StringComparison.Ordinal` parameter")
**Caveat:** only if non-obvious (version requirement, correctness risk)
```

**Rules for compact output:**
- **No ❌/✅ code blocks** for trivial fixes (adding a keyword, parameter, or type change). A one-line fix description suffices.
- **Only include code blocks** for non-obvious transformations (e.g., replacing a LINQ chain with a foreach loop, or hoisting a closure).
- **File locations as inline comma-separated list**, not a table. Use `File.cs:L42` format.
- **No explanatory prose** beyond the Impact line — the severity icon already conveys urgency.
- **Merge related findings** that share the same fix (e.g., all `.ToLower()` calls go in one finding, not split by file).
- **Positive findings** in a bullet list, not a table. One line per pattern: `✅ Pattern — evidence`.

End with a summary table and disclaimer:

```markdown
| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | N | ... |
| 🟡 Moderate | N | ... |
| ℹ️ Info | N | ... |

> ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** These results are generated by an AI assistant and are non-deterministic. Findings may include false positives, miss real issues, or suggest changes that are incorrect for your specific context. Always verify recommendations with benchmarks and human review before applying changes to production code.
```

## Validation

Before delivering results, verify:

- [ ] All critical patterns were checked (from reference files or inline recipes)
- [ ] Topic-specific recipes run only when matching signals detected
- [ ] Each finding includes a concrete code fix
- [ ] Scan execution checklist is complete (all recipes run)
- [ ] Summary table included at end

## Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Correct Approach |
|---------|-----------------|
| Flagging every `Dictionary` as needing `FrozenDictionary` | Only flag if the dictionary is never mutated after construction |
| Suggesting `Span<T>` in async methods | Use `Memory<T>` in async code; `Span<T>` only in sync hot paths |
| Reporting LINQ outside hot paths | Only flag LINQ in identified hot paths or tight loops; LINQ is acceptable in code that runs infrequently. Since .NET 7, LINQ Min/Max/Sum/Average are vectorized — blanket bans on LINQ are misguided |
| Suggesting `ConfigureAwait(false)` in app code | Only applicable in library code; not primarily a performance concern |
| Recommending `ValueTask` everywhere | Only for hot paths with frequent synchronous completion |
| Flagging `new HttpClient()` in DI services | Check if `IHttpClientFactory` is already in use |
| Suggesting `[GeneratedRegex]` for dynamic patterns | Only flag when the pattern string is a compile-time literal |
| Suggesting `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan` broadly | Only for ultra-hot paths with benchmarked evidence; adds complexity and fragility |
| Suggesting `unsafe` code for micro-optimizations | Avoid `unsafe` except where absolutely necessary — do not recommend it for micro-optimizations that don't matter. Safe alternatives like `Span<T>`, `stackalloc` in safe context, and `ArrayPool` cover the vast majority of performance needs |

</skill-context>

## .NET Performance Analysis: `GreekConverter.cs`

**Hot-path context:** Confirmed — invoice generation, thousands of invoices. All findings elevated accordingly. Target appears to be .NET 8+ (collection expressions, `FrozenDictionary` available).

### Scan execution checklist
| Recipe | Hits |
|--------|------|
| `.ToLower()/.ToUpper()` without culture | **8** (code): L96, L126, L145, L153, L172, L180, L198, L205 |
| Unsealed non-abstract/static classes | **1**: L8 `GreekNumberToWordsConverter` |
| `params` / `new Dictionary<` / `new List<` / `Regex` | 0 |
| Chained `.Replace()` | 0 |
| `static readonly Dictionary<` (FrozenDictionary candidate) | 0 (maps are `string[]` — already optimal) |
| `ToLowerInvariant` (positive) | 1: L253 (helper, correct) |

---

### 🔴 Critical

#### 1. Culture-sensitive `.ToLower()` on a billing hot path (8 instances)
**Impact:** `.ToLower()` uses `CurrentCulture`, so invoice text becomes locale-dependent and non-deterministic across servers/threads. For Greek it also risks final-sigma (`Σ`→`ς`/`σ`) transforms. Worse: **every source string in `UnitsMap`/`TensMap`/etc. is already lowercase**, so all 8 calls are pure waste — each allocates a full copy of the (recursively built) string for a no-op. In deep recursion (e.g. billions) this multiplies allocations at every level.
**Files:** GreekConverter.cs:96, 126, 145, 153, 172, 180, 198, 205
**Fix:** Delete `.ToLower()` at all 8 sites. The map data is already lowercase, so output is unchanged and correctness/allocation both improve. (If any future map entry were uppercase, use `ToLowerInvariant()` like the helper at L253 — never `ToLower()`.)

**Example (L96):**
```csharp
result += ConvertImpl(number % 10, returnPluralized);   // was: .ToLower()
```

---

### 🟡 Moderate

#### 2. Compound `+=` concatenation with interpolation (6 instances)
**Impact:** Each `result += $" {...}"` allocates: the interpolated string + a new concatenated result (plus the now-removed `.ToLower()` copy). On the recursive path these stack up per numeric group.
**Files:** GreekConverter.cs:89, 126, 153, 180, 205 (and interpolated returns L145/172/198)
**Fix:** After removing `.ToLower()`, the remaining cost is inherent to recursion. For the common tens/hundreds path, prefer `string.Concat(a, " ", b)` over `+=` interpolation to drop one allocation. Deeper refactor (threading a `StringBuilder` through the recursion) is optional and only worth it if profiling shows this dominates.

#### 3. Leaf converter class not sealed (1 instance)
**Impact:** `Convert`/`ConvertToOrdinal` are interface dispatches; sealing lets the JIT devirtualize and inline the private helpers. Cheap win, called once per invoice.
**Files:** GreekConverter.cs:8
**Fix:** `public sealed class GreekNumberToWordsConverter`.

---

### ✅ Positive findings
- **Lookup maps** — `static readonly string[]` with collection-expression init: optimal, zero per-call allocation. No `FrozenDictionary` needed.
- **`GreekGrammaticalHelpers.ToLowerSafe`** (L253) — correctly uses `ToLowerInvariant()`; use it as the model for finding #1.
- **No LINQ, regex, `params`, or per-call collection allocations** on the conversion path.

---

| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | 1 (8 sites) | Culture-sensitive + redundant `.ToLower()` |
| 🟡 Moderate | 2 | `+=` interpolation allocations; unsealed class |
| ℹ️ Info | 0 | — |

**Top recommendation:** Removing the 8 `.ToLower()` calls is the single highest-value change — it fixes a correctness bug (locale-dependent invoices) *and* eliminates a string allocation at every recursion level, at zero behavioral cost since the data is already lowercase.

# .NET Performance Patterns

Scan C#/.NET code for performance anti-patterns and produce prioritized findings with concrete fixes. Patterns sourced from the official .NET performance blog series, distilled to customer-actionable guidance.

## When to Use

- Reviewing C#/.NET code for performance optimization opportunities
- Auditing hot paths for allocation-heavy or inefficient patterns
- Systematic scan of a codebase for known anti-patterns before release
- Second-opinion analysis after manual performance review

## When Not to Use

- **Algorithmic complexity analysis** — this skill targets API usage patterns, not algorithm design
- **Code not on a hot path** with no performance requirements — avoid premature optimization

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Source code | Yes | C# files, code blocks, or repository paths to scan |
| Hot-path context | Recommended | Which code paths are performance-critical |
| Target framework | Recommended | .NET version (some patterns require .NET 8+) |
| Scan depth | Optional | `critical-only`, `standard` (default), or `comprehensive` |

## Workflow

### Step 1: Load Reference Files (if available)

Try to load `references/critical-patterns.md` and the topic-specific reference files listed below. These contain detailed detection recipes and grep commands.

**If reference files are not found** (e.g., in a sandboxed environment or when the skill is embedded as instructions only), **skip file loading and proceed directly to Step 3** using the scan recipes listed inline below. Do not spend time searching the filesystem for reference files — if they aren't at the expected relative path, they aren't available.

### Step 2: Detect Code Signals and Select Topic Recipes

Scan the code for signals that indicate which pattern categories to check. If reference files were loaded, use their `## Detection` sections. Otherwise, use the inline recipes in Step 3.

| Signal in Code | Topic |
|----------------|-------|
| `async`, `await`, `Task`, `ValueTask` | Async patterns |
| `Span<`, `Memory<`, `stackalloc`, `ArrayPool`, `string.Substring`, `.Replace(`, `.ToLower()`, `+=` in loops, `params` | Memory & strings |
| `Regex`, `[GeneratedRegex]`, `Regex.Match`, `RegexOptions.Compiled` | Regex patterns |
| `Dictionary<`, `List<`, `.ToList()`, `.Where(`, `.Select(`, LINQ methods, `static readonly Dictionary<` | Collections & LINQ |
| `JsonSerializer`, `HttpClient`, `Stream`, `FileStream` | I/O & serialization |

Always check structural patterns (unsealed classes) regardless of signals.

**Scan depth controls scope:**
- `critical-only`: Only critical patterns (deadlocks, >10x regressions)
- `standard` (default): Critical + detected topic patterns
- `comprehensive`: All pattern categories

### Step 3: Scan and Report

**For files under 500 lines, read the entire file first** — you'll spot most patterns faster than running individual grep recipes. Use grep to confirm counts and catch patterns you might miss visually.

For each relevant pattern category, run the detection recipes below. Report exact counts, not estimates.

**Core scan recipes** (run these when reference files aren't available):
```
# Strings & memory
grep -n '\.IndexOf(\"' FILE                    # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.Substring(' FILE                    # Substring allocations
grep -En '\.(StartsWith|EndsWith|Contains)\s*\(' FILE  # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.ToLower()\|\.ToUpper()' FILE        # Culture-sensitive + allocation
grep -n '\.Replace(' FILE                      # Chained Replace allocations
grep -n 'params ' FILE                         # params array allocation

# Collections & LINQ
grep -n '\.Select\|\.Where\|\.OrderBy\|\.GroupBy' FILE  # LINQ on hot path
grep -n '\.All\|\.Any' FILE                    # LINQ on string/char
grep -n 'new Dictionary<\|new List<' FILE      # Per-call allocation
grep -n 'static readonly Dictionary<' FILE     # FrozenDictionary candidate

# Regex
grep -n 'RegexOptions.Compiled' FILE           # Compiled regex budget
grep -n 'new Regex(' FILE                      # Per-call regex
grep -n 'GeneratedRegex' FILE                  # Positive: source-gen regex

# Structural
grep -n 'public class \|internal class ' FILE  # Unsealed classes
grep -n 'sealed class' FILE                    # Already sealed
grep -n ': IEquatable' FILE                    # Positive: struct equality
```

**Rules:**
- Run every relevant recipe for the detected pattern categories
- **Emit a scan execution checklist** before classifying findings — list each recipe and the hit count
- A result of **0 hits** is valid and valuable (confirms good practice)
- If reference files were loaded, also run their `## Detection` recipes

**Verify-the-Inverse Rule:** For absence patterns, always count both sides and report the ratio (e.g., "N of M classes are sealed"). The ratio determines severity — 0/185 is systematic, 12/15 is a consistency fix.

### Step 3b: Cross-File Consistency Check

If an optimized pattern is found in one file, check whether sibling files (same directory, same interface, same base class) use the un-optimized equivalent. Flag as 🟡 Moderate with the optimized file as evidence.

### Step 3c: Compound Allocation Check

After running scan recipes, look for these multi-allocation patterns that single-line recipes miss:

1. **Branched `.Replace()` chains:** Methods that call `.Replace()` across multiple `if/else` branches — report total allocation count across all branches, not just per-line.
2. **Cross-method chaining:** When a public method delegates to another method that itself allocates intermediates (e.g., A calls B which does 3 regex replaces, then A calls C), report the total chain cost as one finding.
3. **Compound `+=` with embedded allocating calls:** Lines like `result += $"...{Foo().ToLower()}"` are 2+ allocations (interpolation + ToLower + concatenation) — flag the compound cost, not just the `.ToLower()`.
4. **`string.Format` specificity:** Distinguish resource-loaded format strings (not fixable) from compile-time literal format strings (fixable with interpolation). Enumerate the actionable sites.

### Step 4: Classify and Prioritize Findings

Assign each finding a severity:

| Severity | Criteria | Action |
|----------|----------|--------|
| 🔴 **Critical** | Deadlocks, crashes, security vulnerabilities, >10x regression | Must fix |
| 🟡 **Moderate** | 2-10x improvement opportunity, best practice for hot paths | Should fix on hot paths |
| ℹ️ **Info** | Pattern applies but code may not be on a hot path | Consider if profiling shows impact |

**Prioritization rules:**
1. If the user identified hot-path code, elevate all findings in that code to their maximum severity
2. If hot-path context is unknown, report 🔴 Critical findings unconditionally; report 🟡 Moderate findings with a note: _"Impactful if this code is on a hot path"_
3. Never suggest micro-optimizations on code that is clearly not performance-sensitive

**Scale-based severity escalation:**
When the same pattern appears across many instances, escalate severity:
- 1-10 instances of the same anti-pattern → report at the pattern's base severity
- 11-50 instances → escalate ℹ️ Info patterns to 🟡 Moderate
- 50+ instances → escalate to 🟡 Moderate with elevated priority; flag as a codebase-wide systematic issue

Always report exact counts (from scan recipes), not estimates or agent summaries.

### Step 5: Generate Findings

**Keep findings compact.** Each finding is one short block — not an essay. Group by severity (🔴 → 🟡 → ℹ️), not by file.

Format per finding:

```
#### ID. Title (N instances)
**Impact:** one-line impact statement
**Files:** file1.cs:L1, file2.cs:L2, ... (list locations, don't build tables)
**Fix:** one-line description of the change (e.g., "Add `StringComparison.Ordinal` parameter")
**Caveat:** only if non-obvious (version requirement, correctness risk)
```

**Rules for compact output:**
- **No ❌/✅ code blocks** for trivial fixes (adding a keyword, parameter, or type change). A one-line fix description suffices.
- **Only include code blocks** for non-obvious transformations (e.g., replacing a LINQ chain with a foreach loop, or hoisting a closure).
- **File locations as inline comma-separated list**, not a table. Use `File.cs:L42` format.
- **No explanatory prose** beyond the Impact line — the severity icon already conveys urgency.
- **Merge related findings** that share the same fix (e.g., all `.ToLower()` calls go in one finding, not split by file).
- **Positive findings** in a bullet list, not a table. One line per pattern: `✅ Pattern — evidence`.

End with a summary table and disclaimer:

```markdown
| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | N | ... |
| 🟡 Moderate | N | ... |
| ℹ️ Info | N | ... |

> ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** These results are generated by an AI assistant and are non-deterministic. Findings may include false positives, miss real issues, or suggest changes that are incorrect for your specific context. Always verify recommendations with benchmarks and human review before applying changes to production code.
```

## Validation

Before delivering results, verify:

- [ ] All critical patterns were checked (from reference files or inline recipes)
- [ ] Topic-specific recipes run only when matching signals detected
- [ ] Each finding includes a concrete code fix
- [ ] Scan execution checklist is complete (all recipes run)
- [ ] Summary table included at end

## Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Correct Approach |
|---------|-----------------|
| Flagging every `Dictionary` as needing `FrozenDictionary` | Only flag if the dictionary is never mutated after construction |
| Suggesting `Span<T>` in async methods | Use `Memory<T>` in async code; `Span<T>` only in sync hot paths |
| Reporting LINQ outside hot paths | Only flag LINQ in identified hot paths or tight loops; LINQ is acceptable in code that runs infrequently. Since .NET 7, LINQ Min/Max/Sum/Average are vectorized — blanket bans on LINQ are misguided |
| Suggesting `ConfigureAwait(false)` in app code | Only applicable in library code; not primarily a performance concern |
| Recommending `ValueTask` everywhere | Only for hot paths with frequent synchronous completion |
| Flagging `new HttpClient()` in DI services | Check if `IHttpClientFactory` is already in use |
| Suggesting `[GeneratedRegex]` for dynamic patterns | Only flag when the pattern string is a compile-time literal |
| Suggesting `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan` broadly | Only for ultra-hot paths with benchmarked evidence; adds complexity and fragility |
| Suggesting `unsafe` code for micro-optimizations | Avoid `unsafe` except where absolutely necessary — do not recommend it for micro-optimizations that don't matter. Safe alternatives like `Span<T>`, `stackalloc` in safe context, and `ArrayPool` cover the vast majority of performance needs |

</skill-context>

1. # Memory & String Patterns
2. 
3. ### Use ReadOnlySpan\<byte\> for Constant Byte Data
4. 🟡 **DO** assign constant byte arrays to `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` | .NET 5+
5. 
6. ❌
7. ```csharp
8. byte[] data = new byte[] { 0x48, 0x65, 0x6C, 0x6C, 0x6F };
9. ```
10. ✅
11. ```csharp
12. ReadOnlySpan<byte> data = [0x48, 0x65, 0x6C, 0x6C, 0x6F];
13. ReadOnlySpan<int> primes = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13];
14. ```
15. 
16. **Impact: ~100x faster access than static byte[] field, zero allocation.**
17. 
18. ### Use stackalloc for Small Temporary Buffers
19. 🟡 **DO** use `stackalloc` for small, fixed-size temporary buffers | .NET Core+
20. 
21. ❌
22. ```csharp
23. char[] buffer = new char[64];
24. guid.TryFormat(buffer, out int written);
25. ```
26. ✅
27. ```csharp
28. Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[64];
29. guid.TryFormat(buffer, out int written);
30. ```
31. 
32. **Impact: Zero heap allocation, no GC pressure, instant alloc/dealloc.**
33. 
34. ### Use Span.TryWrite for Allocation-Free Interpolation
35. 🟡 **DO** use `MemoryExtensions.TryWrite` to format into `Span<char>` buffers | .NET 6+
36. 
37. ❌
38. ```csharp
39. string formatted = $"Date: {dt:R}";
40. destination.Write(formatted);
41. ```
42. ✅
43. ```csharp
44. Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[64];
45. buffer.TryWrite($"Date: {dt:R}", out int charsWritten);
46. ```
47. 
48. **Impact: Zero heap allocation for formatting operations.**
49. 
50. ### Use Span.Split() for Zero-Allocation Splitting
51. 🟡 **DO** use `MemoryExtensions.Split` for allocation-free string splitting | .NET 9+
52. 
53. ❌
54. ```csharp
55. string[] parts = input.Split(',');
56. ```
57. ✅
58. ```csharp
59. foreach (Range range in input.AsSpan().Split(','))
60. {
61.     ReadOnlySpan<char> segment = input.AsSpan(range);
62. }
63. ```
64. 
65. **Impact: 208 bytes → 0 bytes per split, 2x faster.**
66. 
67. ### Use UTF8 String Literals (u8 suffix)
68. 🟡 **DO** use the `u8` suffix for compile-time UTF8 `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` | .NET 7+
69. 
70. ❌
71. ```csharp
72. byte[] header = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("Content-Type");
73. ```
74. ✅
75. ```csharp
76. ReadOnlySpan<byte> header = "Content-Type"u8;
77. ```
78. 
79. **Impact: 17ns → 0.006ns — eliminates runtime transcoding entirely.**
80. 
81. ### Use ReadOnlySpan\<char\> Pattern Matching with switch
82. 🟡 **DO** use `switch` on `ReadOnlySpan<char>` for allocation-free string matching | C# 11+
83. 
84. ❌
85. ```csharp
86. switch (attr.Value.Trim()) { case "preserve": /* ... */ break; }
87. ```
88. ✅
89. ```csharp
90. switch (attr.Value.AsSpan().Trim())
91. {
92.     case "preserve": return Preserve;
93.     case "default": return Default;
94. }
95. ```
96. 
97. **Impact: Eliminates string allocation from Trim() in switch-based dispatch.**
98. 
99. ### Use params ReadOnlySpan\<T\> to Eliminate Array Allocations
100. 🟡 **DO** add `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` overloads to library methods | C# 13 / .NET 9+
101. 
102. ❌
103. ```csharp
104. public static void Log(params string[] messages) { /* ... */ }
105. Log("Starting", "Processing", "Done");
106. ```
107. ✅
108. ```csharp
109. public static void Log(params ReadOnlySpan<string> messages) { /* ... */ }
110. Log("Starting", "Processing", "Done");
111. ```
112. 
113. **Impact: Eliminates params array allocation. E.g., Path.Join with 5+ segments saves 64 bytes per call.**
114. 
115. ### Avoid Chained String-Returning Operations
116. 🟡 **AVOID** chains of 3+ string-returning method calls that each allocate intermediates | .NET Core+
117. 
118. **Pattern 1: Chained .Replace() calls**
119. 
120. ❌
121. ```csharp
122. string result = input.Replace("a", "b").Replace("c", "d").Replace("e", "f");
123. ```
124. ✅
125. ```csharp
126. var sb = new StringBuilder(input.Length);
127. // single pass replacing all patterns
128. ```
129. 
130. **Pattern 2: Chained Regex.Replace() calls**
131. 
132. ❌
133. ```csharp
134. public static string Underscore(this string input) =>
135.     Regex3.Replace(Regex2.Replace(Regex1.Replace(input, "$1_$2"), "$1_$2"), "_").ToLower();
136. ```
137. ✅
138. ```csharp
139. return string.Create(totalLength, state, (span, s) => { /* write directly */ });
140. ```
141. 
142. **Pattern 3: += string concatenation in loops**
143. 
144. ❌
145. ```csharp
146. string result = "";
147. foreach (var part in parts)
148.     result += separator + part;
149. ```
150. ✅
151. ```csharp
152. var sb = new StringBuilder();
153. foreach (var part in parts)
154.     sb.Append(separator).Append(part);
155. return sb.ToString();
156. ```
157. 
158. **Impact: Eliminates N-1 intermediate string allocations per chain. For `+=` in loops, eliminates O(n²) total allocation.**
159. 
160. ### Cache char.ToString() for Known Character Sets
161. 🟡 **DO** cache `char.ToString()` results when the set of characters is small and known | .NET Core+
162. 
163. ❌
164. ```csharp
165. return symbol.ToString();
166. 
167. foreach (var prefix in UnitPrefixes)
168.     input = input.Replace(prefix.Value.Name, prefix.Key.ToString());
169. ```
170. ✅
171. ```csharp
172. private static readonly FrozenDictionary<char, string> s_charStrings =
173.     new Dictionary<char, string>
174.     {
175.         ['k'] = "k", ['M'] = "M", ['G'] = "G",
176.     }.ToFrozenDictionary();
177. 
178. return s_charStrings[symbol];
179. ```
180. 
181. **Impact: Eliminates one string allocation per char.ToString() call. Significant when called in loops or on hot paths.**
182. 
183. ## Detection
184. 
185. Scan recipes for memory and string anti-patterns. Run these and report exact counts.
186. 
187. ```bash
188. # .ToLower()/.ToUpper() without culture parameter (allocates + culture-sensitive)
189. grep -rn --include='*.cs' -E '\.(ToLower|ToUpper)\(\)' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
190. 
191. # Chained .Replace( calls (3+ on one line — intermediate string allocations)
192. grep -rn --include='*.cs' '\.Replace(.*\.Replace(.*\.Replace(' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
193. 
194. # params in method signatures (array allocation per call)
195. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'params ' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
196. 
197. # LINQ on strings — .All/.Any on IEnumerable<char> (replace with foreach loop)
198. grep -rn --include='*.cs' -E '\.(All|Any)\(char\.' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
199. ```
200. 
201. ### Patterns Requiring Manual Review
202. 
203. - **Boxing via string.Format**: Can't determine argument types from grep — needs type analysis
204. - **`+=` string concatenation in loops**: `+=` matches all types (int, list, event, string) — needs type context to confirm string
205. - **`char.ToString()`**: Requires knowing the variable type is `char` — not reliably greppable
206.

1. # Collections & LINQ Patterns
2. 
3. ### Use FrozenDictionary/FrozenSet for Read-Heavy Lookup Tables
4. 🟡 **DO** use `FrozenDictionary`/`FrozenSet` for collections created once and read many times | .NET 8+
5. 
6. ❌
7. ```csharp
8. private static readonly Dictionary<string, int> s_statusCodes = new()
9. {
10.     ["OK"] = 200, ["NotFound"] = 404, ["InternalServerError"] = 500
11. };
12. ```
13. ✅
14. ```csharp
15. private static readonly FrozenDictionary<string, int> s_statusCodes =
16.     new Dictionary<string, int>
17.     {
18.         ["OK"] = 200, ["NotFound"] = 404, ["InternalServerError"] = 500
19.     }.ToFrozenDictionary();
20. ```
21. 
22. **Impact: ~50% faster lookups than Dictionary, ~14x faster than ImmutableDictionary.**
23. 
24. ### Use Dictionary Alternate Lookup for Span-Based Keys
25. 🟡 **DO** use `GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>()` to avoid string allocation on lookups | .NET 9+
26. 
27. ❌
28. ```csharp
29. string key = headerLine.Substring(0, colonIndex);
30. if (s_dict.TryGetValue(key, out int value)) { /* ... */ }
31. ```
32. ✅
33. ```csharp
34. var lookup = s_dict.GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>();
35. ReadOnlySpan<char> key = headerLine.AsSpan(0, colonIndex);
36. if (lookup.TryGetValue(key, out int value)) { }
37. ```
38. 
39. **Impact: Avoids string allocation per lookup — especially valuable in parser/protocol hot paths.**
40. 
41. ### Use CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef for Lookup-and-Update
42. 🟡 **DO** use `CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault` for dictionary update patterns | .NET 6+
43. 
44. ❌
45. ```csharp
46. _counts.TryGetValue(key, out int count);
47. _counts[key] = count + 1;
48. ```
49. ✅
50. ```csharp
51. ref int count = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(_counts, key, out _);
52. count++;
53. ```
54. 
55. **Impact: ~48% faster for lookup-and-update patterns (95µs → 49µs).**
56. 
57. ### Use Collection Expressions [] for Zero-Allocation Span Creation
58. 🟡 **DO** use collection expressions for `Span<T>` targets | C# 12 / .NET 8+
59. 
60. ❌
61. ```csharp
62. int[] values = new int[] { a, b, c, d };
63. ```
64. ✅
65. ```csharp
66. Span<int> values = [a, b, c, d];
67. ReadOnlySpan<int> daysInMonth = [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31];
68. ```
69. 
70. **Impact: Zero heap allocation for span-targeted collection expressions.**
71. 
72. ### Use EnsureCapacity on List/Stack/Queue Before Bulk Adds
73. 🟡 **DO** call `EnsureCapacity` before bulk insertions | .NET 6+
74. 
75. ❌
76. ```csharp
77. var list = new List<int>();
78. for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)
79.     list.Add(i);
80. ```
81. ✅
82. ```csharp
83. var list = new List<int>();
84. list.EnsureCapacity(10000);
85. for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)
86.     list.Add(i);
87. ```
88. 
89. **Impact: Reduces reallocations and array copies during bulk operations.**
90. 
91. ### Use TryGetNonEnumeratedCount for Pre-Sizing
92. 🟡 **DO** use `TryGetNonEnumeratedCount` to pre-size destination collections | .NET 6+
93. 
94. ❌
95. ```csharp
96. var results = new List<int>();
97. foreach (var item in source)
98.     results.Add(Transform(item));
99. ```
100. ✅
101. ```csharp
102. var results = source.TryGetNonEnumeratedCount(out int count)
103.     ? new List<int>(count)
104.     : new List<int>();
105. foreach (var item in source)
106.     results.Add(Transform(item));
107. ```
108. 
109. **Impact: Avoids O(n) enumeration for counting; eliminates resizing allocations.**
110. 
111. ### Hoist Static Data Out of Method Bodies
112. 🟡 **AVOID** creating collections with static/deterministic data inside method bodies | .NET Core+
113. 
114. ❌
115. ```csharp
116. public string Convert(long number)
117. {
118.     var groupsMap = new Dictionary<long, Func<long, string>>
119.     {
120.         { 1_000_000_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} billion" },
121.         { 1_000_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} million" },
122.         { 1_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} thousand" },
123.     };
124. }
125. ```
126. ✅
127. ```csharp
128. private static readonly FrozenDictionary<long, Func<long, string>> s_groupsMap =
129.     new Dictionary<long, Func<long, string>>
130.     {
131.         { 1_000_000_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} billion" },
132.         { 1_000_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} million" },
133.         { 1_000, n => $"{Convert(n)} thousand" },
134.     }.ToFrozenDictionary();
135. 
136. public string Convert(long number)
137. {
138.     // ... use s_groupsMap
139. }
140. ```
141. 
142. **Impact: Eliminates collection + internal storage + closure allocations per call. For a Dictionary with N entries, saves ~N+3 allocations per invocation.**
143. 
144. ### Add Overloads to Avoid params Array Allocation
145. 🟡 **DO** add 1- and 2-argument overloads for methods that accept `params T[]`, or use `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` on .NET 9+ | .NET Core+
146. 
147. ❌
148. ```csharp
149. public static string Transform(this string input, params IStringTransformer[] transformers) =>
150.     transformers.Aggregate(input, (current, t) => t.Transform(current));
151. 
152. "hello".Transform(To.TitleCase);
153. ```
154. ✅
155. ```csharp
156. // Option A: Explicit overloads for common arities
157. public static string Transform(this string input, IStringTransformer transformer) =>
158.     transformer.Transform(input);
159. 
160. public static string Transform(this string input, IStringTransformer t1, IStringTransformer t2) =>
161.     t2.Transform(t1.Transform(input));
162. 
163. public static string Transform(this string input, params IStringTransformer[] transformers) =>
164.     transformers.Aggregate(input, (current, t) => t.Transform(current));
165. 
166. // Option B (.NET 9+ / C# 13): params ReadOnlySpan<T> — zero heap allocation
167. public static string Transform(this string input, params ReadOnlySpan<IStringTransformer> transformers)
168. {
169.     foreach (var t in transformers)
170.         input = t.Transform(input);
171.     return input;
172. }
173. ```
174. 
175. **Impact: Eliminates one array allocation per call for the common 1- and 2-argument cases. `params ReadOnlySpan<T>` eliminates it for all arities.**
176. 
177. ## Detection
178. 
179. Scan recipes for collection and LINQ anti-patterns. Run these and report exact counts.
180. 
181. ```bash
182. # Static Dictionary not using FrozenDictionary (read-only after init)
183. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'static readonly Dictionary<' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
184. 
185. # Static FrozenDictionary (already optimized — verify the inverse)
186. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'static readonly FrozenDictionary<' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
187. 
188. # Per-call List allocation (inside method bodies, not static/readonly fields)
189. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'new List<' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | grep -v 'static\|readonly' | wc -l
190. 
191. # Per-call Dictionary allocation (inside method bodies, not static/readonly fields)
192. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'new Dictionary<' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | grep -v 'static\|readonly' | wc -l
193. 
194. # StringComparer.CurrentCulture usage (almost always wrong in library code — use Ordinal)
195. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'StringComparer.CurrentCulture' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
196. 
197. # LINQ chains in extension/hot-path files (.Select, .Where, .Cast, .Take, .Aggregate)
198. grep -rn --include='*.cs' -E '\.(Select|Where|Cast|Take|Aggregate)\(' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
199. ```
200. 
201. For the LINQ chain recipe: any hit in a file whose name ends in `Extensions.cs`, `Formatter.cs`, or implements a method called from a public extension method is a hot-path candidate. Inspect each hit in these files and flag LINQ chains that allocate delegates, enumerators, or intermediate collections on every call. Hits in localization converters or one-time initialization are lower priority.
202. 
203. ### Patterns Requiring Manual Review
204. 
205. - **ContainsKey + indexer double-lookup**: Requires verifying the same key is used in a subsequent indexer access — multi-line/multi-statement context
206. - **LINQ on hot paths**: The LINQ chain recipe above catches call sites, but distinguishing hot-path from cold-path requires context. Prioritize hits in `*Extensions.cs` and `*Formatter.cs` files, which are typically called on every user invocation
207. - **`new Dictionary/List<` in method bodies vs fields**: The grep heuristic (`grep -v 'static\|readonly'`) catches most cases but may include false positives from field initializers without `static`/`readonly` — spot-check flagged lines
208.

1. # Structural Patterns
2. 
3. Patterns detected by the **absence** of a keyword or interface. These require codebase-wide counting scans, not single-file matching.
4. 
5. ### Seal Classes for Devirtualization
6. 🟡 **DO** seal all leaf classes (those not subclassed) | .NET Core 3.0+
7. 
8. Sealing lets the JIT devirtualize/inline virtual calls and use pointer comparison for type checks. Every non-abstract, non-static class that is not subclassed should be sealed.
9. 
10. **Detection:** This is an absence pattern — scan for classes that are NOT sealed.

12. ```bash

14. grep -rn --include='*.cs' -E '^\s*((public|internal|private|protected|file)\s+)?(partial\s+)?class ' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | grep -v 'sealed' | grep -v 'abstract' | grep -v 'static' | wc -l
15. 
16. # Count already-sealed classes (verify the inverse)
17. grep -rn --include='*.cs' 'sealed class' --exclude-dir=bin --exclude-dir=obj . | wc -l
18. ```

20. **Exclusions:** Do not seal classes that are subclassed elsewhere in the codebase. Identifying base classes requires manual review — grep for `: ClassName` patterns and cross-reference, but expect false positives from interface implementations and generic constraints.
21. 
22. ❌
23. ```csharp

25. { public override int Run() => 42; }
26. ```
27. ✅
28. ```csharp

30. { public override int Run() => 42; }
31. ```
32. 
33. **Impact: Virtual calls up to 500x faster; type checks ~25x faster. Severity scales with count.**
34.

36. - 1-10 unsealed leaf classes → ℹ️ Info
37. - 11-50 unsealed leaf classes → 🟡 Moderate
38. - 50+ unsealed leaf classes → 🟡 Moderate (elevated priority)

---

## Findings

### 🟡 Moderate

#### 1. String `+=` concatenation in recursive hot path (18 instances)
**Impact:** Each `+=` allocates a new string; combined with recursion, a single `Convert` for a large number allocates dozens of intermediate strings. On a batch hot path this dominates. This is the highest-value fix.
**Files:** MultiLocaleConverters.cs:54–109 (Swedish), 328–359 (Hungarian)
**Fix:** Build with a `StringBuilder` (or `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`) and materialize once at the end. Swedish also does a final `.Trim()` (L114) — a builder lets you avoid the trailing-space/trim allocation entirely by controlling separators.
**Caveat:** Recursive calls return strings, so refactor so the recursion appends into a shared builder, or keep recursion returning strings but assemble the top level via builder. Preserve exact spacing (`"och"`, trailing spaces) — cover with a round-trip test before/after.

#### 2. `static readonly Dictionary` should be `FrozenDictionary` (3 instances)
**Impact:** ~2x faster lookups; these are init-once, never mutated. `using System.Collections.Frozen;` is already imported but unused.
**Files:** MultiLocaleConverters.cs:21 (`OrdinalExceptions`), 155 (`TensMap`), 295 (`OrdinalUnitsExceptions`)
**Fix:** Append `.ToFrozenDictionary()` and change field type to `FrozenDictionary<,>`.
**Caveat:** .NET 8+ only. Do **not** touch `_runtimeCache` (L302) — it's mutated at runtime; freezing it would be a correctness bug.

#### 3. `EndsWith`/`StartsWith` without `StringComparison` (4 instances)
**Impact:** Default overload is culture-sensitive → slower and locale-dependent (a real risk here since strings contain `å/ä/ö/é`). 
**Files:** MultiLocaleConverters.cs:128, 134 (×2), 236
**Fix:** Add `StringComparison.Ordinal`. For the single-char checks on L134 (`"a"`, `"e"`), compare the last char directly: `word[^1] is 'a' or 'e'` — avoids the call overhead entirely.

#### 4. Unsealed converter classes (2 of 2 concrete classes)
**Impact:** Sealing enables devirtualization/inlining of the `INumberToWordsConverter` calls in tight loops.
**Files:** MultiLocaleConverters.cs:9 (`SwedishNumberToWordsConverter`), 283 (`HungarianNumberToWordsConverter`)
**Fix:** Mark both `sealed`. (French base is correctly `abstract`; seal its concrete subclasses in their own files.)

### ℹ️ Info

#### 5. `new List<string>()` without capacity (1 instance)
**Impact:** Minor resize risk; parts count is small and bounded (≤4).

# .NET Performance Patterns

Scan C#/.NET code for performance anti-patterns and produce prioritized findings with concrete fixes. Patterns sourced from the official .NET performance blog series, distilled to customer-actionable guidance.

## When to Use

- Reviewing C#/.NET code for performance optimization opportunities
- Auditing hot paths for allocation-heavy or inefficient patterns
- Systematic scan of a codebase for known anti-patterns before release
- Second-opinion analysis after manual performance review

## When Not to Use

- **Algorithmic complexity analysis** — this skill targets API usage patterns, not algorithm design
- **Code not on a hot path** with no performance requirements — avoid premature optimization

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Source code | Yes | C# files, code blocks, or repository paths to scan |
| Hot-path context | Recommended | Which code paths are performance-critical |
| Target framework | Recommended | .NET version (some patterns require .NET 8+) |
| Scan depth | Optional | `critical-only`, `standard` (default), or `comprehensive` |

## Workflow

### Step 1: Load Reference Files (if available)

Try to load `references/critical-patterns.md` and the topic-specific reference files listed below. These contain detailed detection recipes and grep commands.

**If reference files are not found** (e.g., in a sandboxed environment or when the skill is embedded as instructions only), **skip file loading and proceed directly to Step 3** using the scan recipes listed inline below. Do not spend time searching the filesystem for reference files — if they aren't at the expected relative path, they aren't available.

### Step 2: Detect Code Signals and Select Topic Recipes

Scan the code for signals that indicate which pattern categories to check. If reference files were loaded, use their `## Detection` sections. Otherwise, use the inline recipes in Step 3.

| Signal in Code | Topic |
|----------------|-------|
| `async`, `await`, `Task`, `ValueTask` | Async patterns |
| `Span<`, `Memory<`, `stackalloc`, `ArrayPool`, `string.Substring`, `.Replace(`, `.ToLower()`, `+=` in loops, `params` | Memory & strings |
| `Regex`, `[GeneratedRegex]`, `Regex.Match`, `RegexOptions.Compiled` | Regex patterns |
| `Dictionary<`, `List<`, `.ToList()`, `.Where(`, `.Select(`, LINQ methods, `static readonly Dictionary<` | Collections & LINQ |
| `JsonSerializer`, `HttpClient`, `Stream`, `FileStream` | I/O & serialization |

Always check structural patterns (unsealed classes) regardless of signals.

**Scan depth controls scope:**
- `critical-only`: Only critical patterns (deadlocks, >10x regressions)
- `standard` (default): Critical + detected topic patterns
- `comprehensive`: All pattern categories

### Step 3: Scan and Report

**For files under 500 lines, read the entire file first** — you'll spot most patterns faster than running individual grep recipes. Use grep to confirm counts and catch patterns you might miss visually.

For each relevant pattern category, run the detection recipes below. Report exact counts, not estimates.

**Core scan recipes** (run these when reference files aren't available):
```
# Strings & memory
grep -n '\.IndexOf(\"' FILE                    # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.Substring(' FILE                    # Substring allocations
grep -En '\.(StartsWith|EndsWith|Contains)\s*\(' FILE  # Missing StringComparison
grep -n '\.ToLower()\|\.ToUpper()' FILE        # Culture-sensitive + allocation
grep -n '\.Replace(' FILE                      # Chained Replace allocations
grep -n 'params ' FILE                         # params array allocation

# Collections & LINQ
grep -n '\.Select\|\.Where\|\.OrderBy\|\.GroupBy' FILE  # LINQ on hot path
grep -n '\.All\|\.Any' FILE                    # LINQ on string/char
grep -n 'new Dictionary<\|new List<' FILE      # Per-call allocation
grep -n 'static readonly Dictionary<' FILE     # FrozenDictionary candidate

# Regex
grep -n 'RegexOptions.Compiled' FILE           # Compiled regex budget
grep -n 'new Regex(' FILE                      # Per-call regex
grep -n 'GeneratedRegex' FILE                  # Positive: source-gen regex

# Structural
grep -n 'public class \|internal class ' FILE  # Unsealed classes
grep -n 'sealed class' FILE                    # Already sealed
grep -n ': IEquatable' FILE                    # Positive: struct equality
```

**Rules:**
- Run every relevant recipe for the detected pattern categories
- **Emit a scan execution checklist** before classifying findings — list each recipe and the hit count
- A result of **0 hits** is valid and valuable (confirms good practice)
- If reference files were loaded, also run their `## Detection` recipes

**Verify-the-Inverse Rule:** For absence patterns, always count both sides and report the ratio (e.g., "N of M classes are sealed"). The ratio determines severity — 0/185 is systematic, 12/15 is a consistency fix.

### Step 3b: Cross-File Consistency Check

If an optimized pattern is found in one file, check whether sibling files (same directory, same interface, same base class) use the un-optimized equivalent. Flag as 🟡 Moderate with the optimized file as evidence.

### Step 3c: Compound Allocation Check

After running scan recipes, look for these multi-allocation patterns that single-line recipes miss:

1. **Branched `.Replace()` chains:** Methods that call `.Replace()` across multiple `if/else` branches — report total allocation count across all branches, not just per-line.
2. **Cross-method chaining:** When a public method delegates to another method that itself allocates intermediates (e.g., A calls B which does 3 regex replaces, then A calls C), report the total chain cost as one finding.
3. **Compound `+=` with embedded allocating calls:** Lines like `result += $"...{Foo().ToLower()}"` are 2+ allocations (interpolation + ToLower + concatenation) — flag the compound cost, not just the `.ToLower()`.
4. **`string.Format` specificity:** Distinguish resource-loaded format strings (not fixable) from compile-time literal format strings (fixable with interpolation). Enumerate the actionable sites.

### Step 4: Classify and Prioritize Findings

Assign each finding a severity:

| Severity | Criteria | Action |
|----------|----------|--------|
| 🔴 **Critical** | Deadlocks, crashes, security vulnerabilities, >10x regression | Must fix |
| 🟡 **Moderate** | 2-10x improvement opportunity, best practice for hot paths | Should fix on hot paths |
| ℹ️ **Info** | Pattern applies but code may not be on a hot path | Consider if profiling shows impact |

**Prioritization rules:**
1. If the user identified hot-path code, elevate all findings in that code to their maximum severity
2. If hot-path context is unknown, report 🔴 Critical findings unconditionally; report 🟡 Moderate findings with a note: _"Impactful if this code is on a hot path"_
3. Never suggest micro-optimizations on code that is clearly not performance-sensitive

**Scale-based severity escalation:**
When the same pattern appears across many instances, escalate severity:
- 1-10 instances of the same anti-pattern → report at the pattern's base severity
- 11-50 instances → escalate ℹ️ Info patterns to 🟡 Moderate
- 50+ instances → escalate to 🟡 Moderate with elevated priority; flag as a codebase-wide systematic issue

Always report exact counts (from scan recipes), not estimates or agent summaries.

### Step 5: Generate Findings

**Keep findings compact.** Each finding is one short block — not an essay. Group by severity (🔴 → 🟡 → ℹ️), not by file.

Format per finding:

```
#### ID. Title (N instances)
**Impact:** one-line impact statement
**Files:** file1.cs:L1, file2.cs:L2, ... (list locations, don't build tables)
**Fix:** one-line description of the change (e.g., "Add `StringComparison.Ordinal` parameter")
**Caveat:** only if non-obvious (version requirement, correctness risk)
```

**Rules for compact output:**
- **No ❌/✅ code blocks** for trivial fixes (adding a keyword, parameter, or type change). A one-line fix description suffices.
- **Only include code blocks** for non-obvious transformations (e.g., replacing a LINQ chain with a foreach loop, or hoisting a closure).
- **File locations as inline comma-separated list**, not a table. Use `File.cs:L42` format.
- **No explanatory prose** beyond the Impact line — the severity icon already conveys urgency.
- **Merge related findings** that share the same fix (e.g., all `.ToLower()` calls go in one finding, not split by file).
- **Positive findings** in a bullet list, not a table. One line per pattern: `✅ Pattern — evidence`.

End with a summary table and disclaimer:

```markdown
| Severity | Count | Top Issue |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| 🔴 Critical | N | ... |
| 🟡 Moderate | N | ... |
| ℹ️ Info | N | ... |

> ⚠️ **Disclaimer:** These results are generated by an AI assistant and are non-deterministic. Findings may include false positives, miss real issues, or suggest changes that are incorrect for your specific context. Always verify recommendations with benchmarks and human review before applying changes to production code.
```

## Validation

Before delivering results, verify:

- [ ] All critical patterns were checked (from reference files or inline recipes)
- [ ] Topic-specific recipes run only when matching signals detected
- [ ] Each finding includes a concrete code fix
- [ ] Scan execution checklist is complete (all recipes run)
- [ ] Summary table included at end

## Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Correct Approach |
|---------|-----------------|
| Flagging every `Dictionary` as needing `FrozenDictionary` | Only flag if the dictionary is never mutated after construction |
| Suggesting `Span<T>` in async methods | Use `Memory<T>` in async code; `Span<T>` only in sync hot paths |
| Reporting LINQ outside hot paths | Only flag LINQ in identified hot paths or tight loops; LINQ is acceptable in code that runs infrequently. Since .NET 7, LINQ Min/Max/Sum/Average are vectorized — blanket bans on LINQ are misguided |
| Suggesting `ConfigureAwait(false)` in app code | Only applicable in library code; not primarily a performance concern |
| Recommending `ValueTask` everywhere | Only for hot paths with frequent synchronous completion |
| Flagging `new HttpClient()` in DI services | Check if `IHttpClientFactory` is already in use |
| Suggesting `[GeneratedRegex]` for dynamic patterns | Only flag when the pattern string is a compile-time literal |
| Suggesting `CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan` broadly | Only for ultra-hot paths with benchmarked evidence; adds complexity and fragility |
| Suggesting `unsafe` code for micro-optimizations | Avoid `unsafe` except where absolutely necessary — do not recommend it for micro-optimizations that don't matter. Safe alternatives like `Span<T>`, `stackalloc` in safe context, and `ArrayPool` cover the vast majority of performance needs |
